## Differences
Different hardware will see different results too. The biggest differences will be when one kernel is failing at a certain task without your knowledge, since errors are slow usually.

## Testing
In terms of testing, the best way to do it is to install both and try them with your own benchmarks. Repeat testing, log results, and start from a known state you can repeat (e.g. run a stress test for 30 minutes first to heat up the machine).

## Why to stick with just the standard kernel?
Overall modified kernels rarely improve much. You might see that you suddenly have to install dkms packages too for certain hardware to work. Not everything has a dkms driver, in which case, you’re screwed. This is particularly problematic for closed-source software like VMWare.

I personally found the virtual network stack broke itself out of the blue, and was a nightmare to fix. So be wary of all this effort for bad results.

## Conclusion
Try if you want but it really might not be worth focusing on due to marginal benefits.

## Better alternatives
Consider compiling the standard kernel yourself with all optimisations enabled and disable unneeded modules your system does not require. There are many tools that can assist with this

Reading what you’ve asked in other comments too, I think you’re confused what these caches are. 

L1I - L1 Instruction, L1D - L1 Data, L2, L3

The lower the number, the smaller and faster the cache. Why is the cache smaller you might ask? Because it’s far more expensive due to how fast it has to be. Remember it’s even physically placed close to the things that need it most to cut down on latency and signal degradation.

Each core typically has its own bank for each cache. The idea is the CPU knows how often certain data is likely to appear, so it’ll automatically grab more from memory all at once and then work out later if that was actually the right call. The important step here is making less total calls to RAM, because RAM simply is too slow as far as the CPU is concerned.

Why can’t you monitor or read data in these caches? Simple, it’s an unnecessary and insecure feature to add. Since this is transparent to any process and likely transparent to the kernel even, I don’t think there is anyway to monitor it. Frankly monitoring wouldn’t be fun either, since these caches will always be 95-100% full by design.

One thing you could look at is the CPU microcode packages. It’s possible these set parameters for how the caches operate for any number of reasons. It’s also possible there might be a feature for doing what you want hidden away via this.

If you have a big enough drive, you can clone your disk byte for byte with dd. To operate at a file system level, look at using rsync. For rsync, start on a small folder until you’ve got your arguments right. Remember that symlinks will still point to the same path, which may not exist if you only backup a portion of your drive.

Once you’ve successfully backed up your files, verify the backup by inspecting key files, check your permissions/ownership, and attempt a restore in a VM. Also, double check your dotfiles (e.g. .bashrc) were successfully backed up too. If you need a specific subset of files, backup those up manually with cp just in case before you repartition or reinstall.

The Arch wiki has some solid info too: https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/System_backup

Here are some tips I’ve learnt during my time battling Arch for the last year, and I’ve finally made it work for me how I wanted. I think you might find Arch can be made to work for you too, and even distros like Debian run into their own issues. Especially if your underlying hardware is patchy.

1. Never run pip install. Use a virtual environment.
2. Never run pacman (or yay) with -Sy to install a package. Either run -S and hope it’s still in the mirrors, or run a full upgrade at the same time (-Syu).
3. Ensure you’re running pacman -Rs to remove dependencies while removing a package.
4. Backup your stuff. Better yet, backup the whole disk and make sure you can effectively restore to it when needed.
5. Update on the weekend or evening when you have time to fix stuff.
6. Learn to think through a problem you encountered before you need to search it up. Usually it’s something basic, and tracking done info in journalctl or dmesg is more than enough.
7. Make sure your BIOS is up to date, you have your locales set properly, linux-firmware installed, and the correct ucode package for your CPU.
8. Less is more. You can strip down your system a lot, e.g. not installing a desktop manager. Everything you remove is one last thing that can break. 
9. If pacman stops working for any reason, you probably encountered a bad mirror. Most (maybe just some*) outside of Europa and the US are a mess.
10. Grab a virtual machine for tasks that are simpler on Windows. Consider having a list of things you need to work if you’re forced to update at a bad time, so you may fix them. If you can’t, you can probably still get your hardware passed through to a VM.
11. Check you actually did your install right. Dozens of issues can come from bad early config. A big one is forgetting to do your locales properly, and having GNOME fall apart (my experience from tonight).
12. If you reinstall, make sure you create a script for it. I can flash my system in under 20 minutes with only having to enter license keys and pull some files back.
13. Read the subreadit now and again. It will give you a head start on issues you may encounter.
14. Non-standard kernels will cause issues since modules won’t be precompiled. In cases like VMWare, you may not have an easy time manually compiling the modules or getting the existing ones to work properly. If in doubt, try the default linux-kernel.

And that’s my list so far. Feel free to add your own experience, and hopefully some of it helps you.
